Hijri New Year. Also called the celebration of Muharram, the Islamic New Year marks the beginning of the Islamic lunar calendar and commemorates the Hijra, Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in six hundred twenty-two CE. Unlike Western and most lunar new years, the Hijri New Year is observed quietly and spiritually rather than with festive celebrations. It occurs on the first day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar, advancing approximately eleven days earlier each Gregorian year.

The Islamic calendar is purely lunar, comprising twelve months of twenty-nine or thirty days, causing the Hijri New Year to occur roughly eleven days earlier each Gregorian year. The Islamic calendar is dated from the Hijra, the migration event of six hundred twenty-two CE in the Gregorian calendar, with two thousand twenty-four to two thousand twenty-five corresponding to Islamic year fourteen forty-six. The observance is primarily spiritual and contemplative, with many Muslims spending the day in prayer, reflection, and remembrance of the Hijra's historical and religious significance.

Muharram is one of the four sacred months in Islam, during which warfare and hunting are traditionally forbidden. The tenth day of Muharram, called Ashura, is particularly significant in Shia Islam as the day of mourning for Imam Hussain, the grandson of Muhammad, who was killed in battle. The New Year is observed across the Islamic world with prayer gatherings, Quranic recitations, and reflection, though public festivities are more subdued than Western New Year celebrations. Islamic societies traditionally mark the occasion with family gatherings and special foods, though customs vary widely by region and sect.
